Sideburns
SYD-burnz
noun (Boomer slang)
From Ambrose Everett Burnside (1824–1881), Union general, later governor of Rhode Island and U.S. senator, famous for the bushy whiskers that ran down his cheeks into his mustache with a shaved chin. His style was called burnsides by the 1870s; the syllables were reversed into sideburns by the late 1880s, since they grew on the sides of the face. Long, thick sideburns returned as a Boomer fashion in the 1950s (Elvis) and above all in the late 1960s and 1970s. Burnside commanded the Army of the Potomac at the Battle of Fredericksburg, December 11–15, 1862, a disastrous Union defeat.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sideburns are the whiskers grown down the sides of a man’s face in front of the ears. Elvis wore them in 1956, and by 1972 every young man who could grow them did, the longer and bushier the better. The Christian observation: a family in Fredericksburg has a special reason to know where the word comes from. It is named for General Ambrose Burnside, whose whiskers were famous and whose most famous battle was fought on our own streets in December 1862. Against his officers’ doubts he sent wave after wave of Union soldiers across open ground against Marye’s Heights, and thousands fell at the stone wall. Our Lord asked a question every commander should ask: "what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?" (Luk 14:31). "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Pro 16:18). As for whiskers themselves, Scripture treats hair as a matter of honor and order without making it the measure of a man. Israel was told, "Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard" (Lev 19:27), a command separating God’s people from pagan mourning rites; Paul asks whether nature does not teach that long hair is a shame to a man (1Co 11:14); and Absalom’s magnificent hair (2Sa 14:26) became the snare that caught him. The 1970s made hair a statement of identity. Scripture makes it a matter of modest order, and keeps a man’s glory elsewhere: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

Whiskers down the sides of the face, named (by reversal, 1880s) for Gen. Ambrose Burnside, the Union commander defeated at Fredericksburg in December 1862; a Boomer fashion of the 1950s–70s — hair Scripture treats as order and honor, not identity (1Co 11:14; Pro 16:31).

SIDEBURNS, n. pl. (1880s; Boomer-era fashion 1950s–70s) Strips of hair grown down the sides of a man’s face in front of the ears. From burnsides, after Gen. Ambrose E. Burnside (1824–1881).

Fredericksburg note: Burnside led the Army of the Potomac in the Battle of Fredericksburg (December 1862); the Union assaults on Marye’s Heights failed with heavy loss.

Decode for families: ask Grandpa for a photo from 1974. The sideburns will be in it.

Key Scripture

Luk 14:31 — "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?"

Pro 16:18 — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

Lev 19:27 — "Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard."

1Co 11:14 — "Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?"

2Sa 14:26 — "And when he polled his head, (for it was at every year's end that he polled it: because the hair was heavy on him, therefore he polled it:) he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels after the king's weight."

Pro 16:31 — "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness."

Modern Corruption

The 1970s made hair a badge of identity; Scripture treats it as a matter of modest order and honor, and the word’s namesake — defeated at Fredericksburg — is a sober lesson in counting the cost.

expand to see more

Hair was one of the great battlegrounds of the generation gap. Fathers who wore crew cuts were scandalized by sons with long hair, long sideburns, and beards, and many churches made hair length a test of fellowship. Scripture does speak to hair (1Co 11:14), but it does not make it the center of the Christian life, and churches that did so often drove young people away over inches while neglecting weightier matters. The opposite error was just as real: young men made their hair a declaration of rebellion and identity, which is to make an idol of one’s own head.

The word’s namesake supplies the deeper lesson. Burnside was by most accounts a modest man who did not want high command, and he accepted blame for Fredericksburg afterward. But the battle remains a monument to what happens when a plan is pressed past the point of wisdom. Every Fredericksburg father can walk his son along the stone wall at Marye’s Heights and teach Luk 14:31 — count the cost before the battle — and Pro 16:31 — the only hair that is a crown is the gray head found in the way of righteousness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Gen. Ambrose E. Burnside (1824–1881) → burnsides (1870s, his whisker style) → reversed to sideburns (late 1880s) → Boomer fashion (1950s–70s).
